title_en: Homily on James, the Brother of the Lord, and David, the Ancestor of God
author: Hesychius of Jerusalem
occasion: A homily by Hesychius, priest of Jerusalem, on James the brother of the Lord and David the ancestor of God. The surviving text contrasts Bethlehem and Zion and praises James; David is named only in the title and is not developed in the preserved portion.
argument: Hesychius begins by reflecting that if Christ had not humbled himself and become obedient to death, servants would not have been called kinsmen, nor would the clay have been called father of the potter. He then develops a sustained comparison between Bethlehem, where Christ was born, and Zion, where the Church now receives him, showing how the mysteries of the incarnation are fulfilled in the Church. The homily turns to praise James, the brother of the Lord, as commander-in-chief of the new Jerusalem, leader of the priests, and chief of the apostles, whose brief judgment at the apostolic council settled the question of Gentile inclusion. Hesychius presents James's judgment as the voice of Christ himself, the judge of living and dead, speaking through James as an instrument, and urges the hearers to obey.

outline.move: The homily opens by reflecting on Christ's self-humiliation and then addresses Bethlehem and Zion, contrasting the single guiding star of Bethlehem with the many lights of Zion that guide Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and all nations.

Hesychius continues the Bethlehem–Zion comparison: Bethlehem leavened the bread, but Zion revealed the supper; Bethlehem nourished the calf at the manger, but Zion led it up to the altar; Bethlehem hid Jesus in swaddling clothes, but Zion bared his side to Thomas; Bethlehem has a virgin giving birth with the organs of nature closed, while Zion has a bridal chamber receiving the bridegroom within closed doors.

He asks how to praise James, the servant and brother of Christ, commander-in-chief of the new Jerusalem, leader of the priests, and chief of the apostles, and quotes James's decisive words from the apostolic council.
Hesychius presents James's judgment as the voice of Christ himself, the judge of living and dead, speaking through James as an instrument, and urges the hearers to obey.

key_terms.sense: Zion, the Church or heavenly Jerusalem, contrasted with Bethlehem as the place where Christ's mysteries are now fulfilled.
Bethlehem, the place of Christ's birth, contrasted with Zion as the place of the Church's present mysteries.
Commander-in-chief, a military title applied to James as leader of the new Jerusalem.
Leader or ruler, applied to James as leader of the priests.
Chief or leader, applied to James among the apostles.
To legislate or give law, applied to James's authoritative decision at the apostolic council.
I judge or decide, James's decisive word at the council, presented as the voice of Christ.
Judge, applied to Christ as judge of living and dead speaking through James.
Instrument, used of James as the human instrument through whom Christ the craftsman speaks.
Craftsman or artisan, applied to Christ as the one who works through James.
The Word, Christ as the divine Word who supplies the word spoken through James.
Bridal chamber, used of Zion receiving the bridegroom Christ within closed doors.
Bridegroom, Christ as the bridegroom received by Zion.

scripture: The homily quotes or alludes to Philippians 2:8 (Christ humbled himself, obedient to death) and Acts 15:19 (James's judgment at the apostolic council). LXX book names and Psalm numbering should be used where applicable; citations should be given in modern form, e.g. Philippians 2:8, Acts 15:19.
uncertain: The exact date of the homily within Hesychius's lifetime is not established from the source.
The precise liturgical occasion of the homily is not stated in the source.
The relationship between the title's mention of David the ancestor of God and the surviving text, which does not develop a separate section on David, is uncertain.
The catalogue title 'Homilia i in sanctum Lazarum' appears to be a misattribution or error, as the source text treats James and David, not Lazarus.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The surviving text contrasts Bethlehem and Zion and praises James; David is named only in the title and is not developed in the preserved portion.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀνεγνώσθη Ἡσυχίου, πρεσβυτέρου Ἱεροσολύμων, εἰς Ἰάκωβον, τὸν ἀδελφὸν τοῦ κυρίου, καὶ ∆αυὶδ τὸν θεοπάτορα.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source title mentions both James and David, but the preserved portion only develops Bethlehem-Zion and James; we cannot confirm David is 'named only in the title' versus also in a lost portion.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Hesychius begins by reflecting that if Christ had not humbled himself and become obedient to death, servants would not have been called kinsmen, nor would the clay have been called father of the potter.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὐκ ἂν οἰκέται συγγενεῖς ἐχρημάτιζον, οὐκ ἂν ὁ πηλὸς πατὴρ τοῦ κεραμέως ἐλέγετο
_unresolved_facts.fix: The clay would not have been called father of the potter; the brief reverses the relationship (the source says clay [πηλός] is called father of the potter [κεραμέως], not the other way around).

_unresolved_facts.claim: Bethlehem leavened the bread, but Zion revealed the supper
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Σὺ τὸν ἄρτον ἐζύμωσας, ἀλλ' ἡ Σιὼν δεῖπνον ἀνέδειξε
_unresolved_facts.fix: Bethlehem leavened the bread, but Zion revealed the supper — the brief correctly renders this; however, the brief says 'Bethlehem nourished the calf at the manger, but Zion led it up to the altar' which is correct. (No error here; removing this entry)

_unresolved_facts.claim: Bethlehem has a virgin giving birth with the organs of nature closed, while Zion has a bridal chamber receiving the bridegroom within closed doors
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Σὺ παρθένον ἔχεις τίκτουσαν κεκλεισμένων τῶν ὀργάνων τῆς φύσεως, αὕτη παστάδα κεκλεισμένων τῶν θυρῶν ἔνδον τὸν νυμφίον δεχομένην καὶ ἔχουσαν
_unresolved_facts.fix: Bethlehem has a virgin giving birth with the organs of nature closed, while Zion has a bridal chamber with closed doors receiving and holding the bridegroom within — the brief's 'receiving the bridegroom within closed doors' slightly obscures that ἔνδον ('within') modifies the bridegroom's location, not the doors.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The apostle Thomas, to whom Zion bared Christ's side when he wished to touch it
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: αὕτη δὲ τῷ Θωμᾷ τὴν πλευρὰν βουληθέντι ψηλαφῆσαι ἐγύμνωσε
_unresolved_facts.fix: The apostle Thomas, to whom Zion bared Christ's side when he wished to touch it — actually Zion bared the side (to Thomas who wished to touch); the brief's 'when he wished to touch it' is ambiguous but acceptable. (Re-checking: the Greek says τῷ Θωμᾷ βουληθέντι ψηλαφῆσαι, 'to Thomas who wished to touch'; the brief is acceptable. Removing.)

_unresolved_facts.claim: James's words 'Ἐγὼ κρίνω' are quoted, then Hesychius explains that in James the judge of all, both dead and living, speaks; the first-person voice shifts from James to Christ speaking through him.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: «Ἐγὼ κρίνω»· οὗ τὴν κρίσιν ἀθετεῖν οὐ θέμις... «Ἐν ἐμοὶ γὰρ ὁ πάντων κριτὴς καὶ νεκρῶν καὶ ζώντων φθέγγεται»
_unresolved_facts.fix: The first-person 'Ἐγὼ κρίνω' is James's direct speech from Acts 15:19; then Hesychius comments in third person about James's judgment; then the first-person 'Ἐν ἐμοὶ... φθέγγεται' is Hesychius speaking as James/Christ, or rather the text presents a voice that could be read as James speaking or Christ through James. The brief's description of 'first-person voice shifts from James to Christ speaking through him' is oversimplified — the text quotes James, then comments, then presents a first-person speech ('Ἐν ἐμοὶ...') that is ambiguously James or Christ-through-James.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἐν ἐμοὶ γὰρ ὁ πάντων κριτὴς καὶ νεκρῶν καὶ ζώντων φθέγγεται. Ἐμὸν τὸ ὄργανον, ἀλλ' ὁ τεχνίτης ὑπὲρ ἐμέ.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The voice in u01-rem-close speaks as 'I' with 'my instrument' and 'the craftsman above me' — this is more likely James speaking about Christ speaking through him, or a fused voice, rather than straightforwardly 'Christ speaking through James (quoted)'. The brief's identification is interpretively overstated.
